title: Plan black-box verification of a memory. Include address boundaries, read/write ordering, simultaneous operations, reset, and a reference model
source_notes:
**Answer. **I would first define the memory contract: depth, width, request acceptance, read latency, byte enables, reset behavior, and the result of a read and write to the same address. My scoreboard keeps an independent address-to-data model and updates it only on accepted writes. It predicts each accepted read using the specified ordering and compares the response at its expected time. For uninitialized locations, I track whether the contents are defined rather than inventing an expected zero.

Tests cover first/last addresses, every address bit, walking ones/zeros, all-zero/all-one/checkerboard data, back-to-back accesses, write-read-write ordering, byte masks, simultaneous port accesses, stalls, and reset with requests in flight. Assertions check acceptance and response counts, latency, stable stalled responses, and illegal accesses. Coverage crosses operation, address region, masks, collisions, and reset timing. Reset clears contents only if the specification says so.

title: Verify fairness and correct grants in a round-robin arbiter, including persistent requests and contention
source_notes:
**Answer. **I model the round-robin priority pointer and compare every actual grant against the expected eligible winner. I check that grants are one-hot-or-zero, that a grant corresponds to a request, and that the pointer advances on the specified service event. If the winner stalls, the grant must remain stable when the interface requires it. An idle cycle must preserve or reset priority exactly as specified.

For fairness, hold all requests active and check that each requester is served within N accepted service opportunities for an N-way arbiter. A cycle bound requires a separate assumption that service can complete within a bounded time. Test single requests, every contention combination, newly arriving requests, withdrawn requests, pointer wraparound, reset, and long backpressure. Fixed priority can starve a low-priority requester; round-robin fairness depends on eligible requests and service progress.

title: Build a FIFO verification plan. Test reset, empty/full, simultaneous push/pop, wraparound, overflow/underflow, and data order
source_notes:
**Answer. **I use a queue reference model. Each accepted push appends data and each accepted pop removes and compares the oldest item. The occupancy changes by accepted_push minus accepted_pop. The model must follow the specified full/empty and simultaneous push/pop policy, including whether a full FIFO can accept a replacement push when a pop succeeds and whether an empty FIFO supports bypass.

Test reset, one element, fill to full, drain to empty, repeated pointer wraparound, push/pop together at every occupancy, overflow/underflow attempts, and distinct data patterns. Check no loss, duplication, or reordering; flag accuracy; blocked operations; output stability; and read latency. Cross occupancy boundary, operation combination, stalls, and reset. For an asynchronous FIFO, also vary independent clocks, clock phase, stopped clocks, and reset sequencing.

title: Explain the UVM factory and compare factory-based create() against direct new()
Distinguish type overrides from instance overrides
source_notes:
**Answer. **A type override replaces requests for a registered base type wherever they match. An instance override replaces that type only at a matching creation path. A matching instance override takes precedence over a type override. The replacement should extend the requested class so callers can use the same interface.

```systemverilog
base_driver::type_id::set_type_override(error_driver::get_type());
base_driver::type_id::set_inst_override(
  error_driver::get_type(), "uvm_test_top.env.agent0.drv");
```

For components, the instance path follows the parent hierarchy and creation name. For objects, a useful path requires an appropriate creation context. Set overrides before create(). Reference: [UVM factory reference](https://github.com/accellera-official/uvm-core/blob/main/src/base/uvm_factory.svh)

title: Identify the entry point that starts a UVM test
Explain virtual interfaces and how class-based components gain access to DUT signals
source_notes: **Answer. **An interface is a statically instantiated container for signals, clocking blocks, and modports. A virtual interface is a handle that lets dynamically created classes access that instance. The top passes the handle through configuration; the driver and monitor retrieve it. A clocking block gives explicit sampling and driving timing to avoid races with RTL. A virtual interface does not create another interface or another copy of its signals.

title: Explain a virtual sequencer and when coordinating multiple agents requires one
source_notes: **Answer. **A virtual sequencer usually holds handles to the sequencers of several agents. A virtual sequence uses those handles to coordinate traffic such as programming registers before starting data transfers. The virtual sequencer normally has no driver and does not drive pins itself. It is optional. The test can pass agent sequencer handles directly to a virtual sequence and start that sequence on null.

title: Classify UVM phases as tasks or functions. Explain the purpose of check_phase
source_notes:
**Answer. **build_phase, connect_phase, end_of_elaboration_phase, start_of_simulation_phase, extract_phase, check_phase, report_phase, and final_phase are functions. run_phase and the runtime subphases are tasks. check_phase performs final consistency checks such as an empty scoreboard, no outstanding transactions, and no accumulated failures. It cannot wait for a late response; drain traffic during a task phase before checking.

Reference: [UVM phase reference](https://github.com/accellera-official/uvm-core/blob/main/src/base/uvm_common_phases.svh)

title: Draw a complete UVM testbench and trace the sequencer-to-driver request and completion protocol. Include test, env, agents, monitor, scoreboard, predictor and optional coverage
Implement a monitor that collects data while valid is asserted and publishes a completed transaction when valid falls
Launch five concurrent threads; once four have finished, terminate the remaining thread
Distinguish task-based and function-based phases
source_notes: **Answer. **Function phases complete without consuming simulation time and are suited to construction, connections, and final checks. Task phases can wait for clock edges, delays, or events and perform concurrent stimulus and monitoring. UVM starts run_phase tasks for components concurrently. Keep a task phase alive with an objection until stimulus ends and required responses drain. A forever loop in a monitor does not keep the phase alive.

title: Identify top-down versus bottom-up UVM phase traversal
source_notes:
**Answer. **build_phase traverses top-down, so parents configure and create children before the children build. connect_phase, end_of_elaboration_phase, start_of_simulation_phase, extract_phase, check_phase, and report_phase traverse bottom-up. final_phase traverses top-down. Task phases launch concurrent component processes, so their execution should not depend on a parent-before-child runtime ordering.

Reference: [UVM phase reference](https://github.com/accellera-official/uvm-core/blob/main/src/base/uvm_common_phases.svh)

title: Compare uvm_config_db and uvm_resource_db
source_notes:
**Answer. **uvm_config_db is a typed, hierarchy-oriented configuration interface built on uvm_resource_db. Its context and instance path make it a natural choice for virtual interfaces and agent configuration. uvm_resource_db provides more general named or type-based resource access. Prefer config_db for component configuration; check every get() result and avoid an overly broad wildcard that assigns the wrong interface to several agents.

During build, higher-level config settings have greater precedence; settings at the same level use last-set-wins. After build, settings use the default precedence with last-set-wins behavior. Reference: [UVM configuration reference](https://github.com/accellera-official/uvm-core/blob/main/src/base/uvm_config_db.svh)

title: Explain how factory overrides allow replacing implementations without editing the parent test
source_notes:
**Answer. **A parent creates a base component through base_driver::type_id::create(). A derived test registers an override before that creation, so the same parent code receives a derived driver through the base-class handle. Virtual methods provide the replacement behavior. The parent must use factory creation, and the replacement must implement the expected contract.

```systemverilog
function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  base_driver::type_id::set_type_override(stress_driver::get_type());
  super.build_phase(phase); // Parent may create the environment here.
endfunction
```

Both classes must be factory-registered. If the parent builds an object with new(), an override will not affect it. Reference: [UVM factory reference](https://github.com/accellera-official/uvm-core/blob/main/src/base/uvm_factory.svh)

Match parity of every array item to the parity of its index

Manage fork/join_any, selectively cancel one thread, and wait for others
source_notes:
**Answer. **join_any returns after the first child finishes. It leaves the others running. To cancel only a selected child, capture its process handle and call `kill();` then `wait fork` for the remaining children. This follows the process-class example in IEEE 1800 section 9.7.

```verilog
task automatic selective_cancel();
  process p[3];
  fork begin                      // isolate wait fork from caller's children
    fork
      begin p[0] = process::self(); work(0); end
      begin p[1] = process::self(); work(1); end
      begin p[2] = process::self(); work(2); end
    join_any
    wait (p[1] != null);          // handle may not be assigned yet
    if (p[1].status() != process::FINISHED) p[1].kill();
    wait fork;                    // wait for the survivors
  end join
endtask
```

`join_any` resumes the parent as soon as any child finishes. If `work(0)` takes zero time, worker 0 can finish before worker 1 has run `process::self()`, and calling `status()` on a null handle is a fatal error. `wait (p[1] != null)` prevents that. If worker 1 was the first finisher, it is already complete and the status check skips `kill()`. The outer `fork begin ... end join` isolates wait fork from unrelated children of the caller. disable fork would cancel all remaining descendants of the calling process, so it is inappropriate for selecting just worker 1.

For N threads, spawn in a loop with join_none and an automatic copy of the index, because `join_none` children run after the loop variable has moved on. Then wait for the first finisher with p[x].await() or a mailbox.

Shorter alternative for a fixed set of threads: name each block and disable the selected one by name.

```verilog
task automatic selective_cancel();
  fork begin
    fork
      begin : t0  work(0); end
      begin : t1  work(1); end
      begin : t2  work(2); end
    join_any
    disable t1;
    wait fork;
  end join
endtask
```

This has three limits. First, disable acts on a block's static scope, so it kills every active instance of t1, including those in other concurrent calls of the task. p[1].kill() affects only the one process its handle refers to. Second, threads spawned in a loop share one block name, so you cannot select a single one. Third, if t0 finishes in zero time before t1 starts, disable t1 has nothing to disable and t1 runs to completion. In an interview, give this version for "three threads, cancel one", then say you would switch to process handles for reentrant tasks or N threads.

title: Explain how loop-index capture affects processes launched using fork/join_none

source_notes: **Answer. **Use the complete triple_repeat class in direct example 4 above. Its mask contains exactly three set positions, which all take repeated; every other position takes a different value. This guarantees one triple and seven singletons in a ten-element array. For a different length, resize the array and mask together and keep the repetition count at three.

Constrain instruction sequences to prohibit specified operations within recent valid instructions or overlapping execution intervals
prompt:
In processor and hardware accelerator verification, constrained-random stimulus generators must accurately model pipeline hazards, structural issue restrictions, and execution unit resource conflicts.

Implement SystemVerilog constraints for the following two classic verification scenarios:

### Part 1: History-Dependent Instruction Stream
Define an instruction stream class generating one operation at a time (`ADD`, `SUB`, `MUL`, `NOP`):
1. **Cycle-Based History Window:** Prohibit generating an `ADD` if an `ADD` occurred within the previous 3 clock cycles. Elapsed clock cycles count regardless of whether an operation was valid or a stall (`NOP` counts toward elapsed cycles).
2. **Valid-Instruction History Window:** Prohibit generating a `SUB` if a `SUB` occurred within the previous 3 **valid** instructions (`NOP` represents a pipeline bubble/stall and must be **skipped**).

### Part 2: Non-Overlapping Execution Intervals on Shared Resources
Schedule $N$ multi-cycle operations with random `start` cycles, `finish` cycles, and assigned `resource` IDs:
- Operations assigned to the same execution unit/resource must **not** have overlapping execution intervals.
- Treat intervals as half-open $[start, finish)$ so that an operation may begin in the exact cycle that a preceding operation on the same resource finishes.

---

### Concrete Examples

#### Example 1: Part 1 Sequence Generation Walkthrough
| Cycle | Generated Op | `cycles` Queue (Last 3 cycles) | `valid_ops` Queue (Last 3 valid) | Blocked Next Cycle | Explanation |
|:---:|:---:|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 0 | **ADD** | `[ADD]` | `[ADD]` | `ADD` | ADD enters both cycle & valid queues |
| 1 | **SUB** | `[ADD, SUB]` | `[ADD, SUB]` | `ADD`, `SUB` | SUB enters both queues |
| 2 | **NOP** | `[ADD, SUB, NOP]` | `[ADD, SUB]` | `ADD`, `SUB` | NOP advances cycle count, but is skipped by valid ops |
| 3 | **MUL** | `[SUB, NOP, MUL]` | `[ADD, SUB, MUL]` | `SUB` | 3 cycles passed since cycle 0 ADD, so **ADD is now allowed**; SUB still blocked! |
| 4 | **ADD** | `[NOP, MUL, ADD]` | `[SUB, MUL, ADD]` | `ADD`, `SUB` | ADD allowed by cycle history; pushes cycle 0 ADD out of valid queue |

#### Example 2: Part 2 Resource Scheduling Timeline
```text
Cycle:        0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
Resource 0:          [--- Op A ---)[--- Op B ---)      <- Legal: Op B starts when Op A finishes (cycle 5)
Resource 1:              [--- Op C ---)                <- Legal: overlaps in time with Op A/B, but on different resource
```

title: Constrain 2D matrices to unique row maxima, unique minima, and boundary-dependent neighboring values
Randomize matrix dimensions and perform a 90-degree rotation
Generate a tic-tac-toe board
Verify synchronous and asynchronous FIFO behavior, pointer comparisons, Gray-code crossing, and non-power-of-two depth
source_notes:
**Answer. **For a synchronous FIFO, check accepted push/pop operations against a queue and compute occupancy exactly in its clock domain. A counter or wrap-aware pointers can detect empty/full. For a conventional power-of-two asynchronous FIFO, keep binary pointers locally for RAM addressing, convert them to Gray code for crossing, and synchronize each Gray pointer into the opposite clock domain.

For that conventional design, empty compares the next local read Gray pointer with the synchronized write Gray pointer; full compares the next local write Gray pointer with the synchronized read pointer with its two most significant Gray bits inverted. Confirm whether flags use current or next pointers in the actual RTL. Local one-step Gray transitions must change one bit, but a synchronized pointer may skip several source increments and need not differ by only one bit between destination samples. Flags can be pessimistic because of synchronizer latency. Check CDC structure and physical skew constraints in addition to simulation. A binary counter wrapping directly at a non-power-of-two depth does not generally give a one-bit Gray wrap. Use a reviewed arbitrary-depth scheme or a power-of-two physical ring with separately enforced logical capacity. Changing the modulus alone does not work.

title: Calculate FIFO depth for different producer/consumer clock rates and burst occupancy
Explain blocking versus nonblocking assignment scheduling and race conditions
Test fixed-priority and round-robin arbiters
source_notes:
**Answer. **For fixed priority, predict the highest-priority asserted eligible request and compare it with the grant. For round-robin, add a reference priority pointer and update it at the defined service event. Both need one-hot-or-zero grants, no grants to nonrequesters, correct reset state, and stability while a selected transfer stalls.

Exercise all requester masks for a small arbiter, persistent contention, intermittent high-priority requests, changing eligibility, reset mid-service, and pointer wraparound. Fixed-priority starvation can be expected behavior; round-robin should bound wait in service opportunities under persistent requests and eventual downstream progress. Cross winner, contention mask, previous winner, and stalls. Measure fairness only under the assumptions the implementation promises.

title: Verify valid/ready pipeline stages and backpressure under stalls
Select safe CDC methods for slow-to-fast and fast-to-slow crossings
source_notes:
**Answer. **For a single level that stays stable long enough, use a destination-domain synchronizer, commonly two flip-flops. A slow-to-fast pulse can be sampled only if its width and the destination clock behavior guarantee capture. A short fast-to-slow pulse can be missed entirely, so use pulse stretching with a stated bound, a toggle scheme with a rate bound, or a request/acknowledge handshake.

A handshake is appropriate when every event must arrive despite variable clock ratios. A toggle can lose events if it changes twice before the destination observes the first change. Use a data-stable handshake or an asynchronous FIFO for multibit payloads; independently synchronizing each data bit does not preserve coherence. Also test stopped clocks and reset recovery, rather than assuming clock ratio alone proves a safe crossing.

title: Compare synchronized handshake, recirculation mux, and asynchronous FIFO for wide buses
source_notes:
**Answer. **A synchronized request/acknowledge handshake transfers a stable data word with explicit acknowledgment and backpressure. A recirculation mux keeps the destination register unchanged until a synchronized load control tells it to capture the held source data. That mux arrangement still needs a data-stability protocol and timing constraints; it is not sufficient on its own. An asynchronous FIFO buffers multiple words and supports sustained streams with independent clocks.

Choose a handshake for infrequent configuration or status transfers, and an asynchronous FIFO for a stream that needs buffering and throughput. In a bundled-data handshake, hold the payload until acknowledgment and ensure the data reaches the destination before capture. Check reset alignment and do not reuse a handshake slot prematurely. The wide data bus usually bypasses per-bit synchronizers because its coherence comes from holding it stable while the control crosses safely.

title: Explain metastability, reset synchronization, reconvergence, and CDC constraint consistency
source_notes:
**Answer. **Metastability occurs when a flip-flop samples near a transition and may take longer than usual to settle. Synchronizer stages give extra resolution time and reduce the probability of a metastable value reaching functional logic; they do not eliminate it. RTL simulation cannot measure analog metastability or prove a physical MTBF.

Reset may assert asynchronously when required, but deassert it synchronously in each destination clock domain. Check recovery/removal timing and interactions between independently reset domains. Reconvergence occurs when related signals cross through separate synchronizers and later meet with inconsistent latency; transfer them coherently or use a protocol that tolerates the skew. Keep CDC and STA clock/reset definitions consistent. Review clock groups, generated clocks, synchronizer placement, Gray-bus skew/max-delay requirements, reset paths, and justified waivers. A false path is a timing-analysis instruction, not evidence that a crossing is functionally safe.

title: Distinguish setup and hold analysis and debug clock skew
Explain AXI asynchronous crossing and two-master arbitration
source_notes:
**Answer. **An AXI clock crossing needs transaction-aware buffering, commonly asynchronous FIFOs for channel payloads and their handshake state. Preserve AW, W, B, AR, and R information, outstanding IDs, burst boundaries, and write-address/data association. Synchronizing each AXI signal independently can corrupt a transaction.

For two masters targeting one slave, arbitrate accepted address requests, record ownership, and route responses to the correct master. Masters can reuse the same numeric ID, so append a source tag or maintain an ID mapping table. In AXI4, W has no WID and write-data interleaving is absent; keep each write burst associated with its selected address/owner and handle AW/W arriving independently. Test simultaneous masters, colliding IDs, backpressure on each channel, long bursts, fairness, reset, and unmatched address/data timing. Reference: [Arm AXI specification](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ihi0022/latest/)

title: Build and test master-to-slave address routing, fanout, and register slices
source_notes:
**Answer. **Decode each accepted address against nonoverlapping slave regions and retain the selected destination for the transaction. Keep that route stable while the address stalls and while the burst completes. Return a decode error for unmapped addresses according to the interconnect contract. Response routing must preserve the original master and transaction identity.

Test both ends of every address region, adjacent regions, unmapped addresses, concurrent destinations, colliding IDs from different masters, all burst sizes/types supported, byte strobes, and independent channel stalls. AXI bursts must not cross a 4 KB boundary; also check any narrower target-region restrictions. For register slices, compare end-to-end accepted traffic to catch loss, duplication, sideband misalignment, and reordering. Check throughput and bubble behavior as well as correctness. Fanout must deliver a transaction only to its selected target unless a separate broadcast operation is specified. Reference: [Arm AXI specification](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ihi0022/latest/)

title: Compare same-ID versus different-ID outstanding requests and ordering implications
source_notes:
**Answer. **AXI transaction IDs identify streams that have ordering requirements. For conventional AXI4, read responses for the same master and ID preserve request order; write responses for the same master and ID preserve write-transaction order. Different IDs can permit out-of-order completion, so the scoreboard tracks expected transactions by master, direction, and ID rather than using one global FIFO.

A single read burst's beats remain ordered and end with RLAST. Read and write directions are separate. Using the same numeric ID does not impose a universal ordering between a read and a write. Cross-direction dependencies require the specified completion/ordering mechanism. Check the specific AXI version and target memory attributes. Reference: [Arm AXI specification](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ihi0022/latest/)

title: Compare AXI and APB; explain split transactions
source_notes:
**Answer. **AXI has independent read-address, read-data, write-address, write-data, and write-response channels. It supports pipelined traffic, bursts, and, in full AXI, multiple outstanding transactions identified by IDs. APB is a simpler peripheral interface with a setup phase followed by an access phase; it allows wait states but does not provide AXI-style multiple outstanding transactions or bursts.

APB starts setup with PSEL asserted and PENABLE low, then enters access with PENABLE high; completion occurs when PREADY is high. Address and control remain stable during a waited access. AXI decouples request acceptance from later completion, allowing other requests to proceed while a response is pending. That is often what an interviewer means by a split transaction, but AHB's named SPLIT response is a different protocol mechanism. In an AXI-to-APB bridge, verify serialization, address/data retention, byte strobes where supported, error translation, and backpressure. References: [Arm AXI specification](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ihi0022/latest/) and [Arm APB specification](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ihi0024/latest/)

title: Analyze a reset during an in-flight AXI memory-mapped burst and potential hangs
source_notes:
**Answer. **Reset can erase an accepted address, partial write data, or a pending response. If only one endpoint resets, the other may wait forever for a transaction whose state no longer exists. AXI reset requirements do not define a universal system-level recovery policy for every partially completed transaction, so the reset architecture must say which domains reset together and how abandoned requests are handled.

Test reset before address acceptance, after address acceptance, between write beats, before B, during read responses, and with channel backpressure. Check VALID outputs are cleared as required and reset deassertion follows the local clock rules. For a partial reset, use the specified quiesce, isolation, drain, abort/error, or coordinated-reset mechanism. Clear or reconcile ownership tables, FIFOs, credits, and scoreboards by reset epoch. Do not assume a partially written memory burst is atomic or that reset rolls back earlier writes. A bounded recovery/timeout check detects orphaned requests and hangs. Reference: [Arm AXI specification](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ihi0022/latest/)
